body: This implementation is functional but fails to address the core requirement of transaction management. It lacks atomicity, leading to data inconsistency upon failure.

comments.body: This is a critical failure in transaction management. You are committing the order to the database before ensuring that the subsequent inventory deduction succeeds. If deductStock fails, the order remains in the database, leading to an inconsistent state.

Instead of just logging the error, a production-grade system must ensure atomicity. Either both operations (Order creation and Inventory deduction) succeed, or neither does. Consider using a Transaction Manager or the Saga pattern for distributed transactions.
Similar to the Java implementation, this line commits a change to the state before the entire business process is complete. This violates the Atomicity principle of ACID.

In a real-world scenario, this would lead to ghost orders—orders that exist in the system but were never properly fulfilled because the inventory was not reserved. You need a mechanism to roll back this change upon failure.
